prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Make the diagnosis of migraine with typical sensory aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) on clinical grounds: no red flag is present, so no neuroimaging is needed.

Start sumatriptan 50-100 mg at headache onset (not during the aura), which may be combined with naproxen 500 mg or paracetamol 1000 mg, with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg) for nausea.
Keep a headache and menstrual diary for at least 2-3 cycles to confirm the menstrual relation (attacks from 2 days before to 3 days after the onset of menses).

If predictable perimenstrual attacks still respond poorly to acute treatment, offer perimenstrual prophylaxis on the days attacks are expected: frovatriptan 2.5 mg twice daily or zolmitriptan 2.5 mg two or three times daily (NICE CG150), or naproxen sodium 550 mg twice daily [Holland_2012].

Advise that combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring), including continuous regimens used for menstrual migraine, is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; if contraception is wanted, offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve it for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT or for meningitis, neither of which is present here.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; it has a role only when cardioembolic stroke is in question.
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

differential.key_features: A sensory march over 15-25 min is far slower than an ictal march (seconds to a minute or two); headache follows each episode; no loss of awareness; the side varies.
Positive tingling that marches over minutes, followed by headache, recurring identically for 3 years in a 32-year-old without vascular risk factors: the features of aura, not TIA.
Episodic stereotyped sensory marches are not the temporal pattern of MS attacks; no other neurological deficits
The hand-to-face march crosses dermatomes and peripheral nerve territories: a central (cortical) origin.
The facial heaviness is a sensory description: no weakness of the face, arm or leg in any attack and normal power today, so there is no motor aura.

key_clinical_evidence: A hand-to-face sensory march over 15-25 min with positive tingling, followed by headache, is a typical migraine aura; ictal marches take seconds and TIA symptoms are maximal at onset
Attacks consistently before menstruation: a menstrually related pattern to confirm with a diary; perimenstrual prophylaxis is an option if acute treatment fails
No imaging or laboratory test is needed when ICHD-3 criteria are met and no red flag is present
Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Heaviness without weakness is a sensory description; there is no motor aura, so the criteria, imaging and triptan restrictions of hemiplegic migraine do not apply
red_herrings.data_point: Mild heaviness of the face during the sensory aura
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be read as motor aura and prompt a hemiplegic migraine label, imaging or triptan avoidance

findings.result: About 10-12 stereotyped attacks a year for 3 years.

Sensory only: tingling from the fingertips up the arm to the ipsilateral face, usually left-sided, occasionally right. Facial heaviness; no weakness of the face, arm or leg in any attack. No visual, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Slow march over 15-25 min; resolves fully before the headache.

Throbbing headache, 7-8/10, contralateral to the aura, after the aura resolves, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia; lasts 4-8 h. About 1 headache day a month; work disability (leaves work early).
Attacks consistently in the days before menstruation; diary not yet kept.
Paracetamol 1000 mg moderate relief; one borrowed sumatriptan dose very effective.
Headache-free. Normal cranial nerves, facial sensation, power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. BP 112/70 mmHg.

Systemic symptoms or fever: absent. Neoplasia history: absent. Neurological deficit between attacks: absent. Sudden onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 29). Pattern change: absent. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Pregnancy: not reported. Aura always on the same side: absent. Motor aura: absent. No red flag present.

clinical_assessment.impression: Recurrent fully reversible sensory aura marching over 15-25 min, followed by contralateral headache: meets ICHD-3 1.2.1.1 typical aura with headache (criterion C 5 of 6). Attacks cluster before menstruation. No red flag; no motor aura; normal examination.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 32-year-old Hispanic woman was referred to the neurology clinic by her primary care physician for recurrent episodes of numbness and tingling that she has experienced monthly for approximately 3 years. Each episode begins with tingling in the fingertips of one hand (usually the left, occasionally the right) that slowly marches up the arm to the same side of her face over 15-25 minutes. During this phase she may experience mild heaviness of that side of the face, but she has never had weakness of the face, arm or leg, speech difficulty or visual symptoms during an episode. After the sensory symptoms resolve, she develops a severe throbbing headache on the opposite side (7-8/10) with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound that lasts 4-8 hours. She takes acetaminophen 1000 mg which provides only moderate relief. She has tried sumatriptan once (borrowed from a friend), which was very effective.

She has approximately 10-12 episodes per year, consistently occurring in the days before her menstrual period. She recalls her mother having similar episodes with 'numbness and headaches' that improved after menopause. She works as a school administrator and the episodes frequently interfere with work — she has had to leave early on multiple occasions. She is on no regular medications, has never smoked, drinks wine socially (2-3 glasses/week), and exercises regularly. She reports normal blood pressure at routine checks, no diabetes, no prior stroke or cardiac history, and no recent travel or infections.

On examination today (headache-free), the neurological examination is entirely normal with full strength, intact sensation, normal reflexes, and normal coordination.
